utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue with the examination of the present witness, the Chamber would like to deal with a few issues still outstanding. The first one is of a very practical nature. The Chamber would like to sit next Wednesday in the afternoon instead of in the morning and would just like to know whether there's any opposition either from the Defence or the Prosecution to swap. Yes. And I didn't see you consult with General Galic. He might have appointments or whatever next Wednesday. Is it all right, as far as you're concerned as well, General Galic? Yes. Thank you very much. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No problems from the Prosecution, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll sit next Wednesday in the afternoon instead of in the morning. Then the Prosecution has asked for some extension of time in respect of the submissions made in relation to experts. The Prosecution has asked for extension of time until the 10th of January. The Chamber has not heard any opposition from the Defence side and is -- yes. Since I hear no objections from the Defence, the extra time is granted until the 10th of January. Then we still have the issue of the replacement of witnesses. And I'd like to split that up in two parts. The first part is the request made by the Defence on the 19th of December. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think we requested protective measures, but because of his health, he was not able to appear before this Trial Chamber, just like the other witness, who has been cited as a witness who was to appear in the submission of the 19th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... I just mentioned. The witnesses to replace the other witnesses, are there any requests -- I didn't see any requests for protective measures in their respect. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the moment I haven't requested protective measures. And when I spoke to him, I was informed that he wouldn't be requesting protective measures. But I am waiting for your decision so that they can appear. I can't claim for sure that protective measures won't be requested before he appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... just refer to the two witnesses suggested to replace two other witnesses in your request of the 19th of December. Both new witnesses. The name starts with a "K." The Chamber grants the request. The Prosecution in its response has asked for 60 days of preparation of cross-examination. Could the Defence indicate when they intend to call these two witnesses replacing the other two witnesses. What -- at what time approximately?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would first of all like to inform the Trial Chamber that the Defence counsel has written a submission that will be provided to the Trial Chamber through the Registry today, and in that submission we have given the reasons for which the 60 days which have been requested to prepare to hear these witnesses, this is not a period of time that the Trial Chamber should grant my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was whether you intend to call these witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, we intend to call them in 20 days' time. I'm counting with the schedule for the witnesses for the following days, and with the schedule for the witnesses for the week that commences on the 18th. So that would probably be on the 27th of January or on the 1st of February. That is when Defence counsel would call both witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence is allowed to call these witnesses but not on shorter notice than three weeks. If, for any specific reason, the Prosecution would find itself in a position where once started to investigate the background of these witnesses is not able to finish preparation of cross-examination within these three weeks, the Prosecution may ask for more time to prepare but then, of course, should do it at a moment when it's still possible to reschedule the witnesses. So the starting point is three weeks, but if for any specific reason, and upon good cause shown, the Defence -- the Prosecution would need more time, it should be in due time being brought to the attention of the Chamber. Then we had another request -- an earlier request on which a decision has already been taken on the replacement of four witnesses, where the Chamber has granted the replacement of these four witnesses by three other witnesses and has given an opportunity to the Defence to make further submissions in respect of the witness that would replace Mr. Bezrouchenko who was earlier on the list and the new witness would be Mr. Kruk. The Chamber has asked the Defence to give further information that could demonstrate that this witness, Mr. Kruk, would not repeat evidence already presented by the Defence. The Defence has submitted new information to the Chamber. We have considered the reasons why we asked for this further information. That was that Mr. Bezrouchenko would testify about a lot of specific incidents that did not appear on the summaries of other witnesses. On the basis of the newly provided information, the Chamber does not oppose the calling of Mr. Kruk but not for the three hours as scheduled but for one hour and a half. That would mean that for the original scheduling of these witnesses was Kuksenko, two hours, Demurenko, two hours, Golubev, one hour. That would make five hours. To these five hours now a testimony of the witness by the name of Kruk could add one hour and a half to that. That would make altogether six and a half hours for these four witnesses. Then we have a request for protective measures in respect of several witnesses. We cannot deal with that in open session, so I would like to turn into closed session for a while -- for -- private session would be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. I would just like to say that I know that this is the fax number. And up until now the Defence counsel used this number to contact the Prosecution. But for two days now when I intended to file the submissions -- to provide these submissions, it wasn't functioning. But I know that this is the right number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that both parties will certainly be able to communicate to each other those fax numbers that are functioning properly and are closest to the desks of the one for who it is -- to whom it is addressed. Then we were at the stage of re-examination -- Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. I did have one issue that I would ask for clarification with respect to the witness Kruk in terms of proposed timetable or scheduling for the appearance of that witness because again that would be a witness that we would need to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- Commence our searches on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should have -- I should have dealt with that before. Ms. Pilipovic, do you know when you intend to call the witness Mr. Kruk?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence intends to call this witness for the 18th, so the week commencing after the 18th. And on the 6th of December, in a submission which was also provided to the Trial Chamber, I provided the necessary information for Mr. Kruk. But at that time when I was granted permission, he didn't have a passport. I didn't have any more detailed clarifications, any more detailed information about him. I provided this to my colleagues in time, and the Defence intends to call him after the 18th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After the 18th. But that would be already after -- nine days from now, which is very short. Mr. Mundis, would it be wise to insist on a decision now, or could you try to find out what could be done in the spirit of time. I know that 11 days is less than 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My understanding, Mr. President, is that our unit that does the searches won't do the searches until the witness has been, in effect, approved by the Trial Chamber. So if it -- if the Chamber has ordered this witness, I'll make the inquiries today. I can't speculate as to how quickly it can be done, but certainly we will request that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the Chamber has now decided that the Defence is allowed to call Mr. Kruk as a witness for one hour and a half. Could you please inform us then perhaps tomorrow in order to prevent any unnecessary problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'll certainly do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it you reserve your rights to oppose against this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Short term. Then Ms. Pilipovic or Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is the Defence ready to continue the re-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tsynchenko, can you still hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. The re-examination by against counsel will now continue. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good day once more. Yesterday we were discussing the issue of shelling. I'd appreciate it if you could remember what you indicated yesterday. And with regard to this issue of shelling, I have the following question to put to you. I would appreciate it if you could answer by saying yes or no, if that is possible. Do you know precisely -- do you yourself know where all the command posts were located in Sarajevo; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'll put my question to you again in the following manner: Do you know what Kulin Ban is?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This does not arise from cross-examination. This does not arise from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please respond. The Prosecution says that this does not arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That follows from it, and I will explain why. But could the witness take his headphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please assist. And could you also choose another channel for the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the screen be -- This follows from it because since the witness said that he knew all the command posts, I want to check to see whether he has understood my question correctly by asking him, for example, where the Kulin Ban post was. We know where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think that the objection was about the first question already, that command posts --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But I'll get to that. The question is, when we talk about the shelling of Sarajevo, if one doesn't know where the command posts are, then one could say, "Yes, Sarajevo was shelled," but one cannot know whether within Sarajevo it was a command post or a military target that was shelled. And this is the sense in which I want to put my questions and this is why I think it is relevant with regard to the issue of shelling in general. I think that the witness didn't understand my question very well. Perhaps I expressed myself badly, because perhaps he was thinking of UN command posts and not other command posts, so this is why I would like to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But even then the objection of the Prosecution is not that it's irrelevant but that it does not arise from the cross-examination, that whether targets, military targets or not, was not an issue, that has been dealt with in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the issue of shelling was raised and dealt with in a very precise manner by my learned colleagues when they said that you were present with General Soubirou at these discussions on the shelling of Sarajevo. And these are the points that I want to take up again. This comes out of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, you're telling us that the simple fact that shelling was discussed is a sufficient reason to now put this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, what I'm saying is to the extent that we have mentioned discussions between General Galic and General Soubirou, who was the witness's superior, about the shelling of Sarajevo. And this was discussed in general terms. This gives us the possibility to try and find out what this could -- how this could have been understood at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Piletta-Zanin, there might be certain doubts about the fact that the question that you put to the witness comes out of the cross-examination, arises from the cross-examination. The Trial Chamber will allow you to -- one or two questions, but we're not going to deal with all the command post buildings. So just a question or two. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll put the question to you again from the beginning to ensure that things are clear. I'm talking about command posts of the BH army in Sarajevo at all levels, battalions, brigades, inferior command posts, et cetera, lower command post, et cetera. Do you personally know, yes or no, where all these so-called legitimate targets were located; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that while I was there. Right now it's difficult for me to tell you that or to show you those locations. I don't remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. One question: Can you tell me what Kulin Ban is; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, when we talk about the shelling of Sarajevo in general - and could you please concentrate on my question - could you categorically exclude that at the time of the shelling there was not either a mortar shell at the place of the shelling or enemy troops?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. There was -- the witness did not speak of a particular shelling incident. I wonder whether the witness's earphones should be removed at this stage. In cross-examination, Mr. President, the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the witness still can hear your English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Perhaps if the witness may be taken out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, put in the general way as you did it, everyone could answer that question because, in general, you can never exclude these kind of things. So therefore, if you want to be more specific, we might receive information that could assist the Chamber. But in these general terms - and it's not the first time that we hear this kind of question - the Chamber does not think that it's of great assistance. And at the same time, I think this would meet the objection of the Prosecution as well. So in a more specific way, please ask your question about a subject but not in this general way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke yesterday about an incident that happened on the 22nd of January, 1994 in Alipasino Polje. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the incident when the children were killed? Is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, that's the incident I'm referring to, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know whether close to this area there were any military targets, whether they were troops or the headquarters of an establishment, a factory, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that there were workshops there, and the staff of the brigade was to the north of Alipasino Polje -- or rather, not to the north but to the south if one looks at the map. It was to the south of Alipasino Polje and close to the confrontation line. There were barracks there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And with regard to the shelling, again, witness, were you informed about the movements of troops, the movement of the so-called BH side troops within the city; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Given the answer that you have just provided us with, you wouldn't be able to exclude the possibility that the shelling -- so-called shelling of the city could have been the shelling of troops that were moving; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The witness is being invited to speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me ask you the following question,

utterances.speaker: MR. TSYNCHENKO
utterances.text: Did any information reach you at any time about the presence of troops or the presence of mobile mortars close to the place where the incident Mr. Piletta-Zanin just referred to has taken place, at that very moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. And therefore, I cannot give you an accurate answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that yesterday we were talking about approximately ten minutes. We now altogether took approximately 17 minutes. So could you please conclude in a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I only have two -- or in fact, three questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The first one is -- because it wasn't very clear yesterday: What can you tell us about the direction that fire was coming from with regard to the incident that we are talking about, on the 22nd of January, 1994 in Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In cross-examination, there were no issues of direction of fire elicited through evidence. This is completely new material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Isn't it true that the witness has testified on whether investigations took place and whether he is aware of the results of such investigations? And since the witness also testified that he had not been present when the incident happened, it could have only been by the result of investigations, I take it, that -- but perhaps we could ask him. Mr. Tsynchenko, as far as this incident is concerned we were just talk about, do you have any knowledge as to the source of the projectiles -- or the projectile that landed there? And if you have information, what was the source of that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to concentrate on two issues now. The first one concerns the total zone of exclusion, 20 kilometres around Sarajevo. And the second issue is the famous anti-sniper agreement. Do you know whether General Galic was personally involved in trying to obtain these two agreements and in trying to obtain exclusion of heavy weapons around Sarajevo and the agreement -- and the anti-sniper agreement? Was he personally involved in this during his time in Sarajevo; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. In cross-examination there was no issue of total exclusion zones that was elicited through the evidence firstly. Secondly, Mr. President, the witness did not speak during cross-examination of involvement of any persons other then himself in the -- other than himself and General Soubirou in the anti-sniping agreement negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it's not necessary that in cross-examination every single aspect of the question has been dealt with. The objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you understand my question? It was as follows --

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understood your question. General Galic did participate, but -- and without General Galic's participation, it wouldn't have been possible to either put the weapons in depots or whatever. I was responsible for the technical aspect of the question, that is, we collected the weapons, the bounties, and controlled the removal of the weapons at a distance of 20 kilometres away from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you, therefore, often meet and communicate with General Galic in order to bring about the implementation of the agreements?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we did not communicate often. In the beginning General Soubirou had two or three meetings, and we would be present there. General Rose would also participate in this. But later on more concretely we worked with officers who were General Galic's subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And my very last question, my very last question: When -- I'm talking now about the agreement of the total exclusion zone, when it was agreed, how did the troops under General Galic behave? Did they respect that agreement or whatever?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There was no issue of total exclusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But Ms. Mahindaratne, the issue has been yesterday in cross-examination the preparation and the importance of this type of agreements have been extensively dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then it's not inadmissible to extend to that an agreement which might not be the one mentioned but which is -- which shows some similarity in character.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Your very last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you understand, witness, what I asked you, or do you want me to repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what you're asking me. To begin with, I want to say that if four mortar -- four 120 mortars were in place, that was one matter. Then one would have a squad of British soldiers. The mines were placed in crates, 50 to each one, and they would be then kept by British soldiers, and of course nobody would find that. And when there was the Sheridan tank in the mountains, there were also two artillery weapons. At the third point there were four mortars and two -- no, no, there was a gun battery and two mortars. So these are the places -- these are the points where they were kept and I was personally and where there were UN squads who kept these weapons under their control, and therefore those weapons could not fire and did not fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But, witness, my question was as follows: To your knowledge, did General Galic's troops implement properly this agreement on the total exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the exclusion of weapons was observed, and they complied with it strictly. That is, the agreement of the total exclusion zone and the removal of weapons 20 kilometres beyond Sarajevo. Both these agreements were complied with strictly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does the re-examination -- [No interpretation] -- there seems to be a problem with -- we seem to be hearing Russian, I take it. But switching to French, I hear French. And now I will try to understand the English again, and I hear no Russian any more. So that's -- the problems seem to have been solved. Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions to you, Mr. Tsynchenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think we as Judges are not allowed to play the role of the parties. However, I think that the parties shouldn't mislead the Chamber. It could happen when documents are read only partially. That's why I will ask Ms. Mahindaratne something, because you brought that question during the cross-examination, to clarify something for the Chamber. Please have a look on document Exhibit 1823. Which is the date of that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: 11th January 1994?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes. But we have another date which is crossed out, December. But I agree with you, the date is January 11th, 1994. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is a Defence document though, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes, okay. No, yes. But the question was made by you. Now have a look on 1821.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg Your Honour's pardon. 18 ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: 1821. One-eight-two-one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: You read the fourth part of the first paragraph, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I read out to the witness, Your Honour, the last -- the last part of the document, that is, starting from, "Small arms activity."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes. Could you read that again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "Small arms activity was evident around the PTT building, and on two occasions rounds hit the building itself. One round entered the UNHCR radio room, narrowly missing a civilian."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Okay. That's enough for me. Let's go back to 1823. Please read the number 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yes. Could you -- could you read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: "Attacks on UN personnel, equipment, establishment nil. A number of small arm rounds, 7.62 mm hit the PTT building during the night. One of the --" it is not clear on this -- "penetrating the UNHCR window, narrowly missing a--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I assume it's civilian. "After studying the direction and range to the front line, to the," I think, "impact area, it seems unlikely that this round came from anything" -- anything, I think I would prefer, "other than a BiH weapon."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: My question is: Do you think that this paragraph refers to the same incident already mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I beg Your Honour's pardon, but I really would not be able to say so. The wording is the same, but as to whether it's -- since the dates are 11th January, 1994 -- since the dates are the same, it could well be the same incident. But with all due respect to Your Honour, I did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: No. It is because there was a question about the origin of fire yesterday about -- in this incident. That's why I think that the answer is here. That's why I was saying that it is not a good idea to read partially the documents. Now I have a --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Point taken. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Now I have a question for the witness, again on the shelling of Sarajevo. I will read what you said yesterday in one paragraph. You said -- you were talking about the meetings of General Soubirou with General Galic, and you said: "I know that after the shelling of Sarajevo, he, General Soubirou, would go to General Galic and General Soubirou would talk to him about. Whether this was on paper or not, I cannot tell you this." That was your answer. My question is: When you said "after the shelling of Sarajevo," were you referring to any specific incident or in general the shelling of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try to be more precise. When there is an exchange of fire from Sarajevo and from outside of Sarajevo there are all these reports, and everything is being checked because some people write down the number of incoming; others note down the number of outgoing shots, and all this has to be checked. And then the officer on duty, that is, the operations part, those who were in Sarajevo, they collected this kind of information. And after that the information is signed by the senior operations officer, and it is then sent to the two parties to the conflict in the form of protests, that is, it is sent to the Serb side and to the Bosnian side. But when the fire was intense, for instance like the time when Alipasino Polje was shelled. When there were serious incidents, then General Soubirou always went out to Lukavica in person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you. No more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to seek some clarification regarding some of your answers. You told us and you showed on the map areas affected by shelling, and you said that for instance there were theatre and the library involved as well as other objects of worship. These incidents, these shellings, the destruction, did they take place before you came there or during your term there? Was it before -- that is, before November 1993 until July 1994 or was it before you arrived there, before your term started?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that they were. I simply said I was asked about destruction, and I mentioned the objects that had been destroyed. But they were destroyed before I arrived there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If I understand you well, then, all of this destruction took place before you arrived there. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived there, those -- the principal destruction that took place in Sarajevo had happened before my arrival.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then I'll move on to another subject if I may, and that has to do with the anti-sniping agreement. If I understand you well, you were involved in at least the preparation of this agreement for at least six months. Could you tell us, what was the idea behind this agreement? To protect whom? How did you interpret the sniping activities? Was that part of military activities, that is, were they targeting military facilities or military targets or something else? That is, what was the raison d'etre which led you to prepare this agreement and to try to put such an agreement in place? I mean, of course not only you personally but the United Nations. Why did they embark on this and bring the two sides together to do this?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such an agreement was indispensable because it wasn't only the civilians who were being killed. There were also military who were being killed by snipers on both sides. There were casualties also among the UN troops that were there and military observers. And therefore, this was an agreement which wanted to avoid any casualties, be it amongst the civilians or amongst the military. That was the reason for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So you are confirming to me that at least in part it was to protect the civilian population, but not the others. Yes, yes, yes. Please do. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much. [In English] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got a few questions for you as well. Mr. Tsynchenko, do you know until when General Galic served as commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was still in office at the time when I left. I am not sure. I do not really know until when he served as commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know why he was replaced as a commander of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know. I had no part. I could not really be in this high-ranking Serb headquarters or receive any information from them, and I was not in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you have no information on why he was replaced. Thank you. That was my --

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I have none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You testified that the war sometimes was a guerilla war, where you explained to us that sometimes there was firing within the city of Sarajevo. So not over the confrontation lines but within the confrontation lines, when opposing elements would fire at each other within the lines. Could you tell us, what was the frequency of that? Was that very frequent? Was that exceptional? And could you tell us about your personal experience in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the cease-fire agreement was signed, when the heavy weaponry was removed from Sarajevo, the threat of city shelling stopped, but along the lines of confrontation, especially in Grbavica from the Jewish cemetery, there was a sporadic exchange of fire, from firearms or possibly with the use of rocket launchers. But this was not under control. It could happen ten times in different parts of the city, at night -- during one night, or perhaps there would be only one shot one night. So it is very difficult to say anything about the frequency of these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I understand you well: Are you talking now about firing within -- on the territory of one of the parties? So not targeting the other party but targeting with firearms people within the territory of one party?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Basically this fire was exchanged by the two parties, that is, firing at each other across the confrontation lines. But there was also fire within the city. There was rifle fire there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have told us about that. And I'm interested to know whether that fire within the city -- so not against the other party, but within the city -- firing to targets of your own party, was that sporadic, was that frequent? And could you tell us about your own experience in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see it with my own eyes, but there were reports, reports of the monitors and observers who were within the city, reports coming from battalions which were in the city. All these reports came to our operations department. And on the basis of that, we learnt what was the information, learnt what was the situation, because of course we couldn't go to all parts of the city, especially at night. But as I have said, there was exchange of -- fire was also opened on UN soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm mainly interested not on fire opened on UN soldiers but one member of the BH community firing at another member of the BH community, and then I'm talking about the Federation or the Presidency forces or civilians in the Presidency-controlled area.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I cannot say really. I cannot confirm. What I can say is only what I know. I cannot be more precise than that, because the two parties did not provide that kind of information, that is, about their own losses, about their own casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your -- for this answer. I've got one final question for you: You told us about having seen a tank in Ilidza. Could you tell us by whom was the position controlled when you saw that tank.

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosniak party, because that was their tank. That one tank in south Sarajevo, it was theirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And do you know how many tanks they had?

utterances.speaker: MYKHAYLO TSYNCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the rumour was that it was three or five, but they hid them very carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for your answers. Is there any additional question from the parties arising from the questions of the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a problem with the transcript, but it has nothing to do with questions. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No questions from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Then Mr. Tsynchenko, this concludes your examination before this Chamber. You've answered the questions of both the parties and the Bench. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and giving us these answers, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Tsynchenko out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you allow me, I'd like to say something. I have the impression that on page 23, line 10 - I mean, the English transcript - it seems to me that it is not the correct reproduction. As I'm saying, it is just an impression, because Judge El Mahdi said -- my impression is that Judge El Mahdi was speaking about two parties to this matter, and this does not appear in the wording that we see in the transcript and not "the others" which was added. It seems to me that there is confusion in the transcript. So the answer which was given was given to a question which was slightly different, and I believe we have a problem with the transcript. But I think that there is a slight problem with the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unfortunately I'm not in a position to check the translation because my laptop is not working. But Judge El Mahdi tells me that the answer could create no confusion whatsoever. So even if it was not exactly an answer to -- a properly translated question, then the answer is clear. Yes. May I then ask the Defence whether the Defence is ready to call its -- oh, yes, we first have to deal with the documents. You see that even my routine after two weeks is a bit disturbed. Madam Registrar, could you please guide us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1819, map showing Novi Grad and Ilidza; Exhibit D1820, map marked by witness; Exhibit D1821, daily SITREP for 11 January 1994; Exhibit D1822, daily SITREP, 10 January 1994; Exhibit D1823, daily SITREP, 11 January 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I noticed that only on map 1820 any marking was made. 1819 was unmarked. Does the Defence nevertheless insist where we have already have quite some copies of these maps. So then I conclude that 1819 is not tendered any more, and the other documents, 1820 and the following -- the following numbers that they're admitted into evidence being there are no objections. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness, Mr. Pashchenko, if I'm well informed? Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. We started only at -- after 2.30, so I wonder whether it would be wise to have the break now, perhaps, and then retake our usual schedule. I think that would be the wisest thing to do. So we'll then adjourn until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, is the Defence ready to call --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you going to examine the witness or --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll start, but my colleague will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So my words are translated in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please put on the microphone of the witness, because the interpreters are not able to translate his words. Could you please repeat your answers to my last questions. I took it that you said that you could hear me in a language you understand and it was your own language. I'm also informed that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is my native language, Russian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I also understand that you understand the English language to the extent that you are aware of the content of the solemn declaration that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make. If that is true, if your knowledge of the English language is sufficient to understand these words, I invite you to make that solemn declaration. If, however, you'd prefer to do it in your own language, then I'll first read it, ask it to be translated, and then you will repeat these words. But if you are willing to do it in English, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in order not to waste time, I can read it out in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher now hands out to you the text of the solemn declaration. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Pashchenko. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll first be examined by counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us your name, your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Viktor Petrovich Pashchenko.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: On the 26th of October -- the 26th of October, 1961.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is your educational background.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I have a military education. I am an air gunman, navigator. I was an officer -- a staff officer in charge of internal cooperation and assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pashchenko, could you please tell us when did you become a member of UNPROFOR forces.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I arrived at the mission on the 18th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you arrived there on the 18th of January, 1993, could you tell us where that was and how long did you stay there, starting on January 18th.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Initially we arrived in Zagreb. Two days after that we flew on the UN plane to Sarajevo. We spent three days in the Ukrainian Battalion, after which I was appointed deputy in the cooperation office, and I arrived in the PTT building of the Sarajevo sector headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain there?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I remained in that office until the 30th of August, 1993, at which time I was appointed to the staff office in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how long did you remain at the office in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I remained at our force's office in Zagreb until the 14th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pashchenko, when you arrived in Sarajevo, you told us that you were stationed in the Ukrainian Battalion. Can you tell us where was the Ukrainian Battalion stationed at the time in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: The Ukrainian Battalion was stationed in the Tito barracks in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you remained in that part of town for three days, meaning in the Tito barracks. During those three days, did you move about the barracks and did you know whether there were any other troops billeted there in that barracks?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Since the battalion occupied two buildings of the barracks, not counting the cafeteria and the warehouse, I naturally moved about that area during those three days, within the perimeter of the barracks, and other than soldiers of the Ukrainian Battalion, there were no other troops there except for the Dutch communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pashchenko, you told us that after those three days you moved into the PTT building where your office was. Can you describe in detail your workplace in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: My workplace was in an office for cooperation and communications with the warring parties. In that office there was the head of the office, his deputy, and the officers of that department. In total there were five people there from various countries. The office was on the same floor as the office of the sector commander, his deputy, chief of staff, operations centre, and the operations centre of military observers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pashchenko, could you tell us who was the commander of sector at the time when you were there, meaning starting on the 18th of January up until the 30th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I know that at the same time when I arrived Colonel Valentin was appointed sector commander. He was a Frenchman.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And before we get to the issue of your duties when it came to cooperation with warring parties, could you tell us whether you held a rank at the time and what was it.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I was a major at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And what rank do you hold now?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Reserve colonel, since I left the active military service six years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pashchenko, you told us that you worked at the office for cooperation with warring parties. Could you tell us what duties you had there.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I had one single duty from the time I arrived until I left for Zagreb. I was deputy head in the department for cooperation and communications with warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you were deputy head of the department for cooperation with warring parties. Can you tell us, as such, as the deputy head, did you receive protests and upon receiving them did you personally compile reports? Or rather, what were your daily tasks?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I analysed all documents that arrived in our office and were given to the liaison officers, and I forwarded that to the superiors, either to the sector commander or to other superiors. My other duties included negotiations on preparing meetings between superiors in order to reach cease-fire agreements or some other matters. In addition to that, my daily tasks also included efforts put in in order to receive approval from warring parties on the membership of UN missions. Also on convoys that were passing, on engineering missions, movements of UN troops, and similar matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pashchenko, you told us that one of your main tasks was to receive reports from liaison officers of the warring parties. Now, could you tell us where were the offices of liaison officers located and which sides had their liaison officers that you contacted.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: At the time there were three offices for cooperation: On the Croatian side, the side of the Bosnian army, and on the Serbian side as well. They were located on the first floor in the same hallway.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The first floor could also mean the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, the officers of the warring parties that you just mentioned gave you their protests. And based on these protests, you compiled your reports. Could you tell us what was contained in the protests that were given to you by liaison officers of the warring parties? What was their content?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I received not only protests but also the entire information that the officers for cooperation were supposed to give to the sector commander. My role was there simply a member in the chain. I received documents that contained either protests or some proposals and similar things, and then I would pass it on to my superiors. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 17322 to 17329.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you received documents or protests. My question was: What was the content of these protests or documents that you received as simply a person in the chain of communications, the documents that you simply passed on further to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: These were letters written either by the commanders of various warring parties and intended either to the -- to our commander or the sector commander. These letters occasionally contained either proposals for future meetings with various agendas to be discussed. Sometimes those were protest notes in which they protested various activities of the opposing party. So just all kinds of matters that are normally contained in correspondence between the sector commander and the warring sides. Occasionally liaison officers would come directly to the office of the sector commander and deliver letters directly. Therefore, I don't know what was contained in those letters that were directly delivered to the office of the sector commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But you told us that you received protests in which one side protested against the activity of the opposing side. Can you tell us what was normally contained in those protests or what kind of activity of the opposing side was protested.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I received such protests from the officers of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They usually contained information to the effect that today these or those areas of Sarajevo were shelled, as a result of which they were lodging in a protest.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Upon receiving such protests, did you verify whether there indeed was such an incident?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Certainly. In order to do that I visited the operations centre daily and the headquarters of military observers. I received appropriate orders from the battalion and the summary at the operations centre as well as reports from military observers. Then I would compare their data with what I could see on the map, meaning that I would look for confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Upon receiving a protest -- for example, you said that a protest was from the BH army -- and upon verifying that through military observers and the information given to you at the operations centre, did you then, based on that data, compile a daily report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: If I was able to confirm that information, then a protest would be compiled that would be passed on to the liaison officer of the opposing side, the side that was accused of initiating the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Upon compiling a protest of that nature, based on the reports that you had received prior to that and verified, can you tell us whether in this report of yours which later on was sent as a protest to one of the warring parties were there accurate data there as to the targets shelled and the extent of destruction?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: If the information on the extent of destruction and targets was contained in the reports of military observers, then it was included in our protests as well. But mainly we put in only coordinates of the area shelled. Therefore, after verifying and comparing the data with the map, the data contained in the reports, then that data would be included in the protests.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you have just told us that these protests and your daily reports contained only the information concerning coordinates of locations which were shelled and locations from which the fire originated.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: That is correct. We would have the coordinates of the place shelled, and these coordinates were supplied by UN personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When compiling your reports, would you receive and put in the information regarding concrete incidents about the shelling? Did you also receive any information as to possible investigations of such incidents?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, we would receive information if it made part of the remonstrance of the protest of the BH army. This information would be submitted to the sector commander and they would then decide which of the UN parts, which of the links there was to investigate the incident and check whether that incident did indeed happen or not, so that the answer, the response, as to yes, this information has been confirmed or it has been investigated by UN personnel and such and such conclusions can be drawn, such information never passed through my hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you're telling us that during the time of your service there, you have no further knowledge about any investigation conducted of any incident.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us - and I am still referring to the period between the 18th of January to the 30th of August - did you ever receive a report or a protest letter or one of the belligerents concerning something that had happened at a place which then caused casualties or fatalities of a number of soldiers? Did you ever receive such report or shall I call it a protest?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes. From the signals officer of Bosnia and Herzegovina I would receive such information, but that information came from them, that is, without any corroboration by UN personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive reports from your military observers that in a particular part of the city of Sarajevo controlled by the Muslim forces about incidents with major casualties, be it civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Military observers, if they had such information, they submitted it to their headquarters, from which it then went to the upper rung and, therefore, could not possibly get to my office for cooperation, because such information went beyond our terms of reference, our jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your term at your workplace did you ever receive information either from the belligerents or from the military observers that an incident had taken place in a part of the city where there had been a football match and that a number of people perished there, that is, were either wounded or killed? Did you ever receive information related to a football match?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I didn't. I never received such a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally - if you didn't get such a report, then you tell us you didn't - did you hear about such an incident whilst you were in the PTT?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, these are two different things, to get an official report and the hearsay. True, I did not hear about this incident. Yes, I did hear about some other incidents but not about this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you heard some other things about some other incidents. Can you tell us what incident or incidents did you hear about. And if you did, did you get an official report or did you see an official report about such an incident or such incidents during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes. There was this incident when a mine exploded amongst people who were queuing for water, and another one which went off near a bus stop where people were waiting to move on, waiting for the bus or a tram.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us about these two incidents, that you'd heard about them, can you tell us, did, to your knowledge, a report come to your sector saying that an investigation had been conducted of these incidents? And if so, do you know who conducted such an investigation?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Such information did not pass through my office.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pashchenko, when you told us that you received protest letters from the belligerents and that on the basis of reports received from military observers, specifically when you went out to check such protests, that coordinates would be put in, can you tell us if you personally were familiar with the deployment and positions of the parties to the conflict in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: We marked only the confrontation lines on our maps, and we never had the deployment of the two parties to the conflict. And as far as I understand those things, it could not be done at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pashchenko, are you telling us that you did not have information specifically about the deployment of troops and the command posts of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: The information on the location of the headquarters, be it main headquarters or the brigades, yes, we did have that on our map. But specifically regarding the positions, no, we did not have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you had drawn on the maps the command posts of the brigades, if I understand you well, but that you did not have other command posts, does this mean that all the subordinate command posts - I mean, those inferior to the brigade command posts - that you were not aware of their location?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I did not know it, since the minimum -- we indicated only the brigade headquarters and upper rungs, and that was the minimum that we put in.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pashchenko, did you know which were the buildings where the brigade command posts were and in which part of the city were they, if you can remember, of course, approximately? Will you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember that, because even at that time I wasn't really interested in knowing where were their practical positions, since I worked with the representatives of the parties of the conflict to avoid any misunderstanding, any suspicion that I might be conveying information from one party to the other. I simply could not ask for or even receive such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your term, during your tour of duty there, did you have any knowledge as to the weaponry available to the parties of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: There was the UN manual for that, and it listed all the existing weaponry that was at the disposal of the parties of the conflict. The quantities, I, of course, did not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you're telling us that during your tour of duty you were not in a position to see the weaponry used, say, by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: You know, to all intents and purposes, I went to the headquarters at Lukavica once or maybe twice a day. But all I could see were light weapons, that is, those weapons which the military carried with them. I never visited any positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You tell us that you went to Lukavica. Can you tell us what was your cooperation with the liaison officer like? First in the PTT and later on in Lukavica when you went there.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Since it was indispensable to receive the consent of the to-go men for the UN units to perform their tasks, every day we would submit a request with a plan explaining what the UN was planning to do the next day. And daily I would accompany the Serb liaison officer to Lukavica across the confrontation line because that was what one had to do at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pashchenko, when you tell us that you did not visit the positions of the belligerents, can you tell us if during your tour of duty in Sarajevo and at your workplace you became familiar with the positions of the parties to the conflict. Or concretely, I will ask you, did you know where the positions of the BH army were?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: No, I could not, because I did not have that kind of information. As far as I know, not even the operations centre had such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, may I ask you -- I've listened now to this testimony for approximately 40 minutes. It came into my mind, that is, if you were asking mathematical matters to a historian or medical matters to a -- or someone who is very good in building houses. Why would you not ask what the witness knows and what he learned while performing his duties instead of asking for 40 minutes now what he does not know because it was not within his competence but in the competence of other people? Evidence may be very important if it relates directly to the tasks and the duties of a person. Ignorance in other fields might be of less assistance for the Chamber to understand. We'd really like to be fed with information that assists us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I understand that. And I'm trying my best by asking these questions, since the witness spoke about coordinates and maps and in view of the time he spent in Sarajevo, I deem that on the basis of such information he was in a position to know the positions of the parties to the conflict --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to discuss it. But please keep these things in mind when examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pashchenko, when you told us that on the basis of the coordinates which you received from your battalions, can you also tell us if you knew the deployment of the battalions from which you received the reports about certain places, certain coordinates that had been shelled?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: What is specifically at a place indicated by the coordinates, that is something I did not know, except, of course, for that part of Sarajevo where I happened to be, that is, the area between the PTT building to the Ukrainian Battalion and the part of Sarajevo between the PTT building via the airport to Lukavica. Therefore, when I found locations marked by coordinates on the map, then of course I could imagine what was there, what kind of buildings, whether they were skyscrapers, residential buildings, or something else, or perhaps whether it was an unbuilt area.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pashchenko, when you told us that you were familiar with the area around the PTT building and the area around the Ukrainian Battalion, did you ever during your tour of duty -- were you ever present at an incident when weapons were used by either party?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, once. I was with the Ukrainian Battalion, and another time -- that is, when I was at my workplace or in a room where I lived in the sector headquarters, I witnessed the beginning of fire from different types of weapons, either a sporadic fire or sporadic shots.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever present at the incident which happened near your building, when weapons mounted on a vehicle were used? Did you ever see such a case of weapon use?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Once through the window of the room that I lived in I saw that, because before that a few times I could hear the sound well, realising that mortar shots were being fired in front of our building. So once when there was such a shot I tried to open the window, of course being careful. But I did lean through the window and I managed to see a truck of medium size with a blue canvas, and this canvas was lifted on the opposite side and I heard three mortar shots. And after that the truck left. This happened literally 5 or 10, perhaps, metres from the walls of our building. But basically I witnessed - how shall I call it? - incoming shots, both when I was with the Ukrainian Battalion, at the headquarters, that is, or when I was in the PTT building. Likewise, when I arrived in Sarajevo, and having been briefed to always seek shelter, because there were sporadic exchanges of fire and snipers were active. In February 1993, towards the end of the day, that is, at dusk, I was quite often on the PTT building roof. And I would spend there 40, 50 minutes just listening to what was happening. Also, I heard incoming and outgoing shots. Only once I heard an incoming shot, an explosion --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pashchenko, you told us to be more concrete, more precise. When you mentioned this moving, shall I call it, truck, did you personally receive information -- first, did you see men driving that truck, and did you have information as to which army used that type of trucks and which army fired from such a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: No. Since the truck was parked quite near us and I was watching it from the second floor, I could not see whether there was anyone in this truck and the canvas was up on the other side, so that I could not see who was under that canvas. As I have said, it was a medium-sized civilian truck with the blue tarpaulin, with the blue cover, nothing special. I mean, you know, this was just an ordinary truck. Such trucks are used by -- can be used by anybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But did you see in which direction was fire opened from such a truck?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: My windows overlooked skyscrapers in the area called Alipasino Polje, so that the shots were being fired in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pashchenko, if the Defence shows you the map of the city of Sarajevo, could you point at places where coordinates were marked and where the positions of the two parties to the conflict were?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: As I have already told you, the coordinates or the positions, I did not know. I did not know where the positions were. I know the contours of the confrontation lines. I know where the UN battalions were quartered in Sarajevo. But the positions of the belligerents, I did not know them. If you mean the coordinates of the incident that I told you about, that I can show you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague will now continue with the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm looking at the watch. When will we have the next break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In approximately a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Could we show an exhibit, which will be the map, with the assistance of the usher. Mr. President, it's a black-and-white copy of the map that we usually use, but there is only one copy, and I would be grateful if the usher could position it as best as possible to make it visible on the screen. What we are interested in, naturally, is the position of the PTT building; that is to say -- it's the left part of the map, the western part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you recognise this map?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes. This is the map of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, would you be able to indicate the PTT building that you were in? Could you indicate this on the map?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes. I know where the building is. This is where it is located.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness pointed to the building that we are familiar with. Does everyone have the map? I'll wait for a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1824. And may we have copies for the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a certain number of copies. I think that they are over there. I'm afraid that the registrar has -- Madam Registrar has too many copies now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, now that we all have the map, could you please indicate again the location of the building, the one that you said was the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, there's really no need, if we are talking about the PTT building where the headquarters of the UN were, to ask it twice to the witness, unless you expect the witness to testify about another PTT building where he was located different from anyone else. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The matter wasn't clear for me. But if the matter is clear, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you indicate from the PTT building that you pointed to, could you indicate the direction of fire that you referred to a minute ago. A minute ago you mentioned a direction of fire. Could you please indicate this direction by using your pointer.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: My room -- or rather, the windows of my room faced the south side of that building, and the direction of the fire was directed towards the south, across Alipasino Polje. I don't know the exact direction. Plus or minus 15 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But I would appreciate it if -- we can't see anything any more. It would be good if we could see the Alipasino Polje, if we could have a broader view. Again, what we can now see on the screen, witness, I would appreciate it if you would trace the direction on the map, by using the pointer first of all, very roughly.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I believe that it was approximately in this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please take a marker that you will be provided with and trace a line on the axis that you have just indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just ask you -- witness, it should be a black -- black, not any other colour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I believe that this axis was in the central direction. But it could have been also more to the left or to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the moment we can leave this map -- no, just a minute. Thank you. We could have a look at the eastern part of the map now. Thank you. Not the hills, in fact. It's the town that we are interested in. And if possible, the part of the town -- not the hills. There we are. That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you indicate in this part of the map with number "1" the location of the Ukrainian Battalion. Could you indicate this, please.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: As I have already said, the Ukrainian Battalion was stationed in the Tito barracks. I believe that it's either here or here.
