utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can you mark the zone that you have pointed out to with a number "1," the zone that corresponds to the Tito barracks, using a black felt-tip, of course?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you do the same thing, witness, for the Egyptian Battalion, if you are able to locate it. Use the pointer first of all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: The Egyptian Battalion was in Bistrik area, the so-called Bistrik area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Mark it with a number "2."

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, you spoke a minute ago about the positions of brigades. Do you know where the 10th Brigade was located? And this concern it is most important brigades.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: To be honest, it's very difficult to recall the numbers of the brigades as well as their deployment and the locations of the flags on the maps. I know that two of them, two flags, as far as I can remember, were near the Ukrainian Battalion and the Egyptian one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Ukrainian -- very well. Thank you. When you say "two flags," that means one near to the Ukrainian Battalion and one close to the Egyptian Battalion; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to go back to the Bistrik zone, witness. Does the name Caco mean anything to you; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Does the name Commander Caco mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to put the map aside. We will have another look at it later. But I would like to show the witness some other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Exhibit 1825.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any copies available for the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, obviously. But they are in the process of being distributed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, there is an R number on the document. Would that still ask for ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The case manager, Miss McCreath, is checking that at the moment, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Rule 70 clearance for this document has not been lifted, so we would respectfully request that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then go into -- if the document would have to be put on the ELMO, then we would have to go into -- it was already on the ELMO. It was not on the ELMO? This document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I then order that this picture on the ELMO would not be -- does that have to be done in a written decision or ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber gives the order that the -- for the very, very short moment that the document has been put on the ELMO, that this will not be broadcasted. And we turn now into private session, and the document should not be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to put the same question to you about this document, the form of this document. I think you can recognise it; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would now like to concentrate on page 556, and the item concerned is J. This is the period from the 12th to the 18th of February, 1993, which is the period that you were familiar with. This concerns point 1, that starts with the word "Sarajevo." Have you had the time to read what is under item 1?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to make sure, first of all, your knowledge of the English language is sufficient to understand this document which is in the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that you asked the witness also to read point 1 as it continues on page 557, because under G1, it seems to have been highlighted in one way or the other, what is not on the next page. So could you please verify up to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I saw the witness turn the page, and I asked him to read what is under item 1, from G1 up until G2. I think he understood me and that he did this. If this is not the case, he could take some more time to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The second page, 557, would be useful to understand the matter. I can see that the witness is nodding. Witness, what I'm interested in here is the incident which occurred -- with regard to the point called Papa 5. The first question is: Do you know where Papa 5 was located; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's an observation platform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us where it is?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I can indicate that location on a map with a good degree of accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. We will see about that later if it is necessary. Thank you. Perhaps we will do that later. With regard to this incident, were you informed of it while you were in Sarajevo, were you informed of such accidents, such firing accidents; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, but probably --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat. We didn't hear the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- the interpreters asked the witness to repeat the last part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was informed about such incidents, but probably not about all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, with regard to the incident that this document deals with, my first question is: Do you remember this incident precisely; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Here it states that a protest was lodged with a member of the military and that this member of the military said that punitive measures would be taken. Can you confirm this; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I wasn't in the position to know that, because senior military observer acted according to his own discretion and instructions given by the superiors. I didn't participate in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Later on were you aware of the fact that the member of the military in question apparently said that punitive measures would be taken; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: We discussed various cases with military observers there, and there were not many military observers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. But my question was as follows -- I will rephrase it, and if you could answer by saying yes or no, I would appreciate that,

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: that the member of the military who was contacted by your department apparently stated that punitive measures would be taken; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to hand out a document, which bears the number 1827, one-eight-two-seven. It's a document of the same kind, but it has an "R" on it, unless it's an "A." So perhaps we have a problem before we put it on the ELMO. But perhaps it's not even necessary for us to put it on the ELMO, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if we discuss the content of the document, we should turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Rule 70 restriction has been lifted with respect to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we can remain in open session. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In this document -- I think it's on the screen now, witness. I can see a lot of things on the screen now. Thank you, and the usual question, yet again: Do you recognise this kind of document?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please have a look at page 2, which has the number 187 at the end. Thank you. You've got it. What we are interested in in particular is item A on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution would object to this document being shown to the witness on the grounds that it on its face was created after the witness's departure from the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am perfectly well aware of the fact that there is this problem as far as the chronology and the dates are concerned, but we know that the witness remained in the area of Bosnia in a sense since at the time he was in the Zagreb HQ, and my question does not concern the facts that are described under item A. It concerns the location with regard to these facts. And I think that the witness can talk about this in very clear terms. Does this clarify the matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mundis, would you still stick to your objection or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It certainly will depend on the precise questions that are asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's then -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you're allowed to proceed. We'll hear the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The reason is the following: To begin with, witness, did you have time to read item 1 -- item A? Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I'm about to finish it, yes. Yes, I've finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is as follows: We have here somewhere what I will now read to you: [In English] "Serbs have retaliated by heavy shelling in the old part of the city." [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The question is as follows: In relation to these attacks, such a document -- this document talks about the old city. Now, what does that mean, since we do not have the proper topographic reference, that is, we do not have the coordinates here?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I dealt with this document directly, since in Zagreb I was the duty officer of the operations centre there. And since I was on duty round the clock, as any other duty officer, it was my duty to go through all such documents which we received from UN forces and then compiling the report on behalf of the UNPROFOR as such as a whole for New York and for Geneva. Therefore, in response to your question, I can tell you that the old part of the city, in this particular case, meant the area around the Egyptian Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The area which is around the Egyptian building, was it the -- also area which we can define as the area of Bistrik, as far as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Last question regarding this document, witness: In the area of Bistrik, do you know if there were some Belgian [as interpreted] Brigade command posts?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: As I have already said, the map only said brigade headquarters not far from where the Egyptian Battalion was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, we've finished -- we're done with this document. Perhaps we shall come back to it. But I hope you still have before you the previous document -- no, no. Perhaps we'll come to it later. We'll come to that. Now I would like to ask you some questions concerning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was just wondering, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the transcript says -- says something about a Belgian brigade. Did you say BiH or -- I didn't follow you in French. BiH?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I smile because we're not talking about the Belgian army but we're talking -- we can only talk about -- I remember saying the BH, BH Battalion. Yes, I'm sorry. I was not following the transcript. Thank you very much for noticing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like you to tell us if during your tour of duty in Sarajevo you were able to travel frequently, to move about the city. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Not often.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: All right. See, if it is "not often," then how often?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Two, not more than three times a week I visited the Ukrainian Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. And in which zone could you move around?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: During my tour of duty in Sarajevo, UN personnel was forbidden to move freely wherever, so that I went from PTT building to the Tito barracks in an armoured vehicle, and therefore from the PTT to the headquarters at Lukavica in an armoured vehicle again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And during those trips, witness, did you see any civilians in the streets; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And insofar as you saw them, what could you tell us about their clothing in general?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, that varies from one man to the other. But generally speaking, people wore what they had. Practically, of course, at times their clothes looked as if coming from different suits, different parts of different suits.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Concretely, did you ever happen to see civilians wearing parts or whole military uniforms; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, if you mean camouflage clothing as part of military uniforms, such as jackets or vests or trousers, yes, one could see people wearing parts of military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And did it apply to both women and men, elderly and younger people, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, women less than men, but I also saw women wearing camouflage vests.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, during your trips around, did you frequently come across such clothes on individuals who did not seem to be military?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. That calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will reword it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How often -- how often did you happen across individuals wearing such different parts of uniform?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Well, every time practically, every time I moved out. In some areas I came across more such individuals, and in other areas, I came across less such individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I would now like to go back to those trips and the destruction of Sarajevo. Since you were stationed in the city and could move around, I'd like you to tell us what was the difference concerning the destruction of buildings between the confrontation lines and other parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that the confrontation -- that I crossed the confrontation line on my way to the airport, there was a difference in that area, because in the area of the confrontation line, there were residential buildings, private houses, that is, and they had become inhabitable [as interpreted]. They were so badly damaged at that time that they were practically inhabitable [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Does your answer mean that did this not hold true of other areas that you knew? For instance, the centre of the city?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: In the centre of the city were mostly high-rise buildings, and the damage done to them was also considerable, but not 100 per cent, such as along the confrontation line. Along the confrontation line, private houses were practically 100 per cent destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And still -- I'm still on the same subject. Did you see with your own eyes, you personally, minarets? I am saying minarets which were targeted and destroyed. Yes or no? By "destroyed," I mean totally annihilated.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. We are still talking about shelling. Did you, Witness, either in Sarajevo or elsewhere in the course of your military career, did you ever see craters caused by mortars; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Since I became a military observer at a later stage, I did see craters made by mortars, so their depth, their size, depended on the soil and the calibre of the projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you ever see in Sarajevo, witness, and on the asphalt craters which have gone through the asphalt or concrete, as the case may be, and at the bottom of which the end part of the shell would still be planted in the soil, that part which we call the stabiliser, the tail fin? Yes or no, did you ever see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'll go back to provocations that you mentioned earlier, that is, that truck with the blue canvas that you described to us. You told us that you saw it near the PTT building. Do you know if that kind of interventions, that is, shots from a mobile vehicle happened several times? Did this happen repeatedly?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: No. That vehicle was stationary. Four shots were fired. And that was a small diameter mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. My question did -- not to find out whether this vehicle was moving or not. Perhaps we have an interpretation problem there. My question was -- had to do with whether this kind of strategy, that is, opening fire from a truck or from around the truck and then leave this site -- is this something that you know happened or did not happen repeatedly; yes or no? Were you aware of such a strategy?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes. So there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, can you tell us if to your knowledge it also happened in other areas, such as in other areas except around the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: According to the information received from battalion officers in the Tito barracks, such cases happened in their area once or twice a month, and the same holds true of the PTT.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm listening to the Russian interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem seems to be -- have been solved, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you from the bottom of my heart. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will now follow up on your answer. Do you know if other -- if other buildings were used as a kind of shelter for such strategic shots?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: If you mean the mortar fire, then I do not know. But in Sarajevo are buildings only. It's not an open field. It's not a forest. So this was the territory which was fired at and from which fire came.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You are a military expert. Why do you think fire was opened under those circumstances? I mean, in the vicinity of your building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. That calls for speculation. And there's certainly no indication that this witness is a military expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please first, having listened to the military explanations, but clarify the military expertise specifically in this field.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps let's -- let's ask it a different way. Mr. Pashchenko, have you any idea on why shots were fired under these circumstances from these positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Being a military man, educated in a manner which allows me to command a regiment, and therefore I was trained -- I learnt about the tactics and conduct of combat. So I think this strategy could pursue two objectives: First, the mobility. And when you are mobile enough, then you suffer a minimum risk of being targeted or hit. And a second objective which perhaps existed - or perhaps it didn't - it could be a planned place from which shots could be fired, or perhaps it was a provocation. Perhaps they were trying to provoke the response fire which would then -- would nearly hit the UN.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'd now like to go back to the question of protests. First, did you or your men receive protests from the Serb side, from the Serb party?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: No. The Serb side never lodged a protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you've just moved to your next subject. I'm looking at the clock. There are approximately 12 minutes remaining for the examination-in-chief. In view of the experience we had during the testimony of this witness, I'll be very strict in limiting you to two hours. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That will suffice. Thank you very much. That will be quite enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'd now like you to focus on the form of protests that were submitted to you from the other side. You did not receive them from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm interested in the protests of the other party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of a protest in writing in which very precise, specific, and detailed information was supplied, such as proof of, say, a sniper, an active sniper - yes or no? - I'm saying which could be proof of a sniper.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Only the UN could really supply something that would be tantamount to evidence, to proof. In such protests there was no concrete information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pashchenko, could you please explain, because I have some difficulties understanding, what do you exactly mean by that there was no concrete information? Are you referring to specific evidence on the incident or on -- where the incident took place or what the incident was actually about? Could you please clarify your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The protests that we -- that my office received did not contain information about sniper activities and casualties, that is, individuals, with their names and the exact location of such incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: To come back to this: When combat happened, when there was a combat, was there a risk of stray bullets; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I believe so. I think so, because there were such bullets which strayed into the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And now a question which has to do with the ricochet. Was there a technical possibility of ricochets; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you tell us that bullets could stray or could ricochet. Is it possible for either -- for them to cause losses, to cause casualties, human casualties; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, when you received information, whatever, about possible fatalities somewhere, could you technically exclude at the level of your office the possibility of a ricochet or a stray bullet; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I have already said that I did not receive such official information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No. But my question is as follows, witness: Technically, when you had information about a wounded or a dead person, could one categorically exclude, yes or no, the possibility, the risk that something -- that this wounding or this death was caused by a stray bullet or a ricochet?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: No. It was impossible to categorically exclude it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel please wait for the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the interpreters are asking whether you'd like to wait until the witness has finished his answer. And may I perhaps remind you what I said to Ms. Pilipovic before. Questions as to whether we could categorically exclude that during the last year someone became wet because of the rain in the Netherlands are really not assisting the Chamber. I'm just making a comparison, because that happens now and then, and I think you have put a question -- these kind of questions some 30, 40, 50, 60 times to witnesses. Perhaps next time if you ask the question you could give the answer yourself, because it's a matter of logic rather than a matter of knowledge, of facts. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'll try to pay attention to logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: To go back to the issue of the airport, witness. Do you know whether the airport was a place where fire was exchanged; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes. It was very frequently reported that the airport zone was under fire of various intensity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, if you know anything about this, where this fire came from, according to what you can remember?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: The airport is located in the -- along the division lines between the two warring parties. And if one looks at the map, those areas were both to the south and to the right of the airport, in the hilly area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if there was any cross-fire between the two camps that were facing each other?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: It seems that that's how it was, because people were on both sides of the confrontation lines firing at each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether the runway at the airport was used by one of the armies to transport military equipment, and in particular weapons?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: The runway at the airport was used only by the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know whether non-UN personnel crossed the airport runway?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Based on the information contained in daily reports, such cases happened at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether these people who did not belong to the UN and who would cross the runway, do you know whether they were also trying to bring something in to Sarajevo? And if you know anything about this, what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, calls for speculation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me put the question a different way to you. Have you any knowledge about people crossing the runway of the airport and bringing, I would say, contraband into Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about contraband. It is clear that people went from here to there and carried something on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know anything about what they carried on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have one minute left, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which won't be used. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, is there -- is the Prosecution ready to start cross-examining the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've got one or two questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first one is: Were protests of civilians also processed through your channels? Because your testimony was mainly about protests about shelling, and I am specifically interested in possible protests of -- concerning sniping coming from civilians.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: It seems that civilian protests went through the civilian police of the UN. My office did not receive such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You earlier testified that if there was any protest about sniping that you would not know the exact places or the names of the victims. Would that mean that there were protests about sniping in a more general sense but not on specific incidents? Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes. It is correct. The protests on shelling certain areas from mortars were sent to us but not reports on incidents concerning specific persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there were protests about sniping in a more general sense? Is that a correct understanding? Because you said previously that no names and specific locations were known if protests were made in respect of sniping.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Protests concerning sniping incidents did not basically exist. Sniping incidents were recorded by military monitors and were reported along the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would like to take you back to one of the documents shown to you, and that is D1827. I think that the restrictions were lifted, is that correct, of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your attention was drawn to the second page, under number A. It reads: "Serbs have retaliated by heavy shelling in the old part of the city." Would you expect these words to have been used if the response would have specifically been targeting the headquarters close to the Egyptian Battalion?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: I would read this to mean that this was a response against the attacking troops and their communications centre, including the position of their headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you understand this to be a purely military response.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR PASHCHENKO
utterances.text: Yes. This was a response meant to stop the attacking troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for your answer. I have no further questions to you. Is there any need to put additional questions to the witness in respect of the issues dealt with by the questions of the Chamber? If not, this concludes your testimony in this court. Mr. Pashchenko, you've answered the questions -- usually I say of both parties, but you've -- since no questions have been put to you by the Prosecution, you've answered the questions of the Defence and the questions of the Bench. I'd like to thank you for coming and giving your answers to these questions, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Pashchenko out of the courtroom. We will now deal with the documents. Madam Registrar, could you please guide us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1824, map marked by witness; Exhibit D1825 under seal, UNPROFOR report; Exhibit D1826, daily SITREP for period 12 to 18 February 1993; Exhibit D1827, report dated 17 October 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since I hear no objections, the documents are admitted into evidence. We have three minutes left, but I was informed -- the Chamber was informed that the Defence was not able to call any further witnesses this week. Is that correct, Ms. Pilipovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would only like to say that the Defence had planned to call three witnesses, but at the last minute the witness who was the first one to appear informed the witness department on Tuesday that he had a fever and was not able to come. We have attempted by contacting the witness department to have the witness who was supposed to come today -- to have him appear, but there was a misunderstanding because a ticket was reserved for him for Saturday. So we are now without a witness for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber understands that under certain circumstances you're running out of witnesses. Perhaps the time taken by the Prosecution to cross-examine the last witness might have surprised you a bit as well. It's always difficult to find a balance between not wasting any time by running out of witnesses and at the same time not to ask the witnesses to come at such an early stage that they have to wait too long. So it is at least understandable why this situation has arisen. Nevertheless, I would urge the Defence to try to take whatever measures that this situation would not occur again. So this is not to blame you for it but not to -- but just an invitation to pay proper attention to avoiding such a situation to arise. That would also mean that there's no need to sit tomorrow, unless one of the parties would have any specific issue to raise. Then we'll adjourn until next Monday - not in the same courtroom - and at 9.00 in the morning. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 7.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 13th day of January, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: witness:  After the incident, did you know -- were you aware of the fact
